video_title: New Somali Piracy Situation is Insane
gist: Somali piracy is resurging in 2026 at the fastest pace since 2012, with four merchant ships (three of them oil tankers) hijacked and held for ransom since April, driven by a naval-attention vacuum created by the Red Sea Houthi crisis and the US-Iran war, collapsed US development aid to Somalia, and new reported Houthi cooperation with pirate networks that never actually disbanded after the 2011 crisis.

insights.claim: Somali pirates hijacked four commercial merchant ships between April and July 2026, putting 2026 on pace for the highest number of piracy-related hijackings since 2012.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: A resumption of hijackings at this pace signals rising transit risk and insurance costs for shipping routing through the Gulf of Aden/Bab-el-Mandeb corridor, which carries 10-15% of global seaborne trade.
insights.quote: putting the pace of Somali piracy related hijackings on course to be the highest this year in more than a decade since 2012.

insights.claim: The Palau-flagged oil tanker Honor 25 was hijacked on 21 April 2026 about 30 nautical miles off Somalia while carrying refined oil toward Mogadishu to relieve an acute fuel shortage there.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Fuel-cargo vessels serving Somalia's own domestic shortage becoming pirate targets shows the crisis is now also disrupting supply into Somalia itself, not just transit trade.

insights.claim: The St Kitts and Nevis-flagged cargo ship Sword, carrying a full load of fertilizer toward Kenya, was hijacked on 26 April 2026 and subsequently converted by the pirates into a mother ship used to launch coordinated speedboat attacks, including the seizure of two Iranian fishing boats in July.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Captured vessels are being reused as force multipliers (mother ships) exactly as in the 2005-2011 crisis, indicating the pirates have retained and redeployed the old operational playbook rather than starting from scratch.

insights.claim: The Togo-flagged oil tanker Eureka was hijacked on 2 May 2026 while anchored off the port of Kana in southern Yemen, and the ransom demanded for its release has reportedly escalated from $3 million to $10 million with no resolution as of the episode's publication.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: An escalating ransom demand well above 2010s norms on a still-unresolved case is a live cost signal for tanker insurers and owners transiting the Gulf of Aden.
insights.quote: The current ransom being demanded by the pirates for the release of the Eureka alone reportedly escalated from $3 million to $10 million.

insights.claim: The Tanzania-flagged oil tanker Asana was hijacked on 17 July 2026 roughly 65 nautical miles southwest of Al Mukalla, Yemen, in the Gulf of Aden.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: A fourth successful hijacking within a few months confirms this is a sustained wave rather than an isolated incident.

insights.claim: None of the four ships hijacked in 2026 had armed security on board, which made them easier targets and mirrors the pre-2011 vulnerability that armed guards later eliminated.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Shipping companies re-cutting armed-security spending directly reopens the vulnerability that private armed guards had closed off after 2011 -- a concrete, monitorable lever for insurers and owners.
insights.quote: none of the ships involved had any armed security on board, which made them easier targets.

insights.claim: At one point in mid-2026, at least six hijacked vessels were being held simultaneously off the Somali coast, and as of end of July the four main hijacked merchant ships still held 67 crew members hostage while ransom negotiations continued.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Simultaneous multi-vessel captivity at this scale hasn't occurred since 2010-2012, indicating pirate operational capacity has already scaled up meaningfully in a single season.

insights.claim: When Somali authorities arrested a suspected pirate leader tied to the Sword hijacking, armed militiamen attacked the police station holding him the next day, triggering a gunfight that killed one policeman and injured another.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Local law enforcement being unable to hold even an arrested pirate leader underscores how weak state capacity remains a binding constraint on any near-term crackdown.

insights.claim: The world's navies have far less bandwidth to police Somali waters than in the 2010s because NATO's European members are focused on Russia and Ukraine, the US has committed naval assets to the Red Sea against the Houthis, and the US war against Iran further reallocated US naval resources -- creating the security vacuum that Somali pirates are now exploiting.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: A structurally thinner global anti-piracy naval presence (versus a temporary lull) implies the current wave could persist or grow rather than self-correct quickly, unlike prior isolated incidents.

insights.claim: The pirates' 2026 hijacking spree began only about seven weeks after the United States launched its war against Iran in late February 2026 and closed the Strait of Hormuz, a timing link the narrator argues is not coincidental.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Ties the piracy wave directly to a specific, trackable geopolitical trigger (the Iran war/Hormuz closure), suggesting piracy risk should be monitored as a downstream consequence of Middle East naval deployments.
insights.quote: I don't believe that it's a coincidence at all that only around 7 weeks after the US launched its war against Iran, Somali pirates began launching their own rapid capture of merchant vessels again.

insights.claim: The Trump administration cut US development aid to Somalia from $476 million in 2024 to $70 million in 2025 and just $3 million in the first three months of 2026, removing an economic alternative that had been offered to coastal Somali communities for decades.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: A near-total collapse in development aid is a direct, quantifiable policy input pushing more economically desperate young men toward piracy as a livelihood -- a factor that could reverse only through renewed aid or economic investment.
insights.quote: In 2024, during the final year of the Biden administration, the US provided Somalia with $476 million worth of development aid, which the Trump administration drastically reduced to just $70 million in 2025. And during the first three months of 2026, they only sent $3 million to Somalia.

insights.claim: Unlike the 2010s coalition that included Russia, China, India, the US and EU cooperating together against Somali piracy, current NATO/EU-Russia hostility over Ukraine makes renewed naval cooperation and intelligence sharing with Russia on piracy effectively unthinkable today.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: The exact multinational coordination that broke piracy's back in 2011-2012 is politically unavailable this time, implying any counter-piracy response will likely be weaker and slower than the historical precedent.

insights.claim: Rising oil prices caused by the Iran war have incentivized Somali pirates to specifically target oil tankers for higher ransom potential, and three of the four vessels hijacked in 2026 (Honor 25, Eureka, Asana) were oil tankers.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Tanker owners and their insurers transiting the Gulf of Aden/Bab-el-Mandeb are the specific segment bearing disproportionate incremental piracy risk in this cycle, not general cargo shipping.
insights.quote: out of the four merchant vessels that have been hijacked by Somali pirates so far in 2026, three of them have been oil tankers.

insights.claim: Rising shipping, insurance, and fuel costs stemming from the Iran war and Houthi attacks in the Red Sea are causing some shipping companies to cut corners on security, including reducing the armed security teams placed aboard their ships, which increases their exposure to piracy.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: A cost-cutting feedback loop -- higher Red Sea/Iran-war costs leading owners to cut the very security measures that defeated piracy last time -- is a specific, monitorable risk factor for maritime underwriters.

insights.claim: US intelligence indicates that on at least two occasions Somali pirates have coordinated directly with Houthi officials to plan attacks on commercial vessels, with the Houthis reportedly agreeing to help arm, train, and share intelligence with Somali pirates to further disrupt regional maritime commerce -- a form of cooperation that did not exist during the 2010s piracy crisis.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: If Houthi-pirate cooperation is real and sustained, it materially raises the sophistication and persistence of the piracy threat beyond a simple economically-driven resurgence, and links Red Sea and Somali coast risk into a single connected threat corridor.
insights.quote: On at least two instances, at least according to US intelligence, Somali pirates are believed to have coordinated directly with Houthi officials to plan their attacks on commercial vessels.

insights.claim: Illegal and unregulated foreign fishing in Somali waters is still estimated to cost Somalia around $300 million a year, compounding the country's existing economic misery and grievance narrative that originally helped legitimize piracy among coastal communities.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: The original economic grievance that seeded piracy in the 1990s-2000s (foreign fishing fleets depleting Somali waters) remains unresolved and quantifiable at scale, meaning the root driver hasn't been addressed even as the security response has.
insights.quote: illegal and unregulated foreign fishing in Somalia's waters is still estimated to be costing Somalia an average of $300 million a year

insights.claim: Somalia's federal government remains overstretched fighting Al-Shabaab and ISIS insurgencies while also contending with the secessionist Somaliland region (recently recognized as independent by Israel) and a de facto independent Puntland administration, leaving it with almost no capacity to police its own coastline against pirates.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Somalia's fragmented sovereignty is a structural, not cyclical, constraint -- meaning international naval presence rather than Somali state capacity will remain the primary check on piracy for the foreseeable future.

insights.claim: At its 2000s-2010s peak, Somali piracy functioned like a startup financing model: outside investors funded boats, weapons, fuel, and equipment upfront in exchange for a share of ransom profits, while recruiters, gunmen, translators/negotiators, and clan elders each filled specialized paid roles.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Understanding piracy as a financed criminal enterprise with an investor/return structure explains why it scales rapidly whenever the expected-ransom-to-risk ratio improves, and why it can collapse just as fast when that ratio flips.

insights.claim: An individual pirate involved in a successful hijacking could earn between $10,000 and $75,000, versus Somalia's average annual income of only around $700 -- meaning a single successful raid could equal a lifetime of ordinary local income.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: The payout-to-local-income ratio is the core economic engine driving recruitment; as long as this gap persists, renewed successful ransoms will keep pulling in new participants regardless of enforcement.

insights.claim: At the 2010-2011 peak, Somali pirates collected only around $100-200 million per year in ransom revenue, while the total worldwide economic cost of Somali piracy reached roughly $6-7 billion annually, driven mainly by higher insurance premiums, security teams, naval deployments, legal costs, and rerouting.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: The ~30-70x gap between pirate revenue and total global economic cost shows piracy imposes a large, diffuse tax on global shipping/insurance far exceeding the actual ransom outflows -- the real cost is borne through insurance and freight markets, not just direct ransoms.

insights.claim: Publicly reported data from the height of the 2010s crisis indicates that not a single merchant ship carrying an armed private security team was ever successfully hijacked once the practice became widespread, which was probably the single biggest factor in collapsing the piracy business model.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Armed private security is the single most effective, historically-proven countermeasure; its adoption rate today is therefore the clearest leading indicator of whether the 2026 wave will be contained or continue growing.
insights.quote: Publicly reported data from the height of the crisis indicates that not a single merchant ship carrying an armed private security team was ever successfully hijacked after the practice became widespread.

insights.claim: Once armed security and naval countermeasures made attacks unprofitable, Somali piracy attacks collapsed extremely fast -- from an all-time high of 237 attacks in 2011 to 75 in 2012, 15 in 2013, 11 in 2014, and zero successful hijackings at all between 2013 and 2016.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: The historical collapse curve shows piracy's investment-driven economics can reverse within one to two years once expected returns fall, which is a useful base rate for how quickly the current 2026 wave could also be suppressed given the right countermeasures.

insights.claim: The pirates, financiers, negotiators, and local support networks from the 2005-2012 piracy boom were never arrested or dismantled -- they simply went dormant (returning to fishing, moving into smuggling, or joining insurgencies) once piracy stopped being profitable, retaining the knowledge and relationships needed to restart operations quickly.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: Because the underlying human capital and networks survived intact, any renewed opportunity (naval vacuum, high ransoms, economic desperation) can reactivate piracy far faster than building a new criminal industry from scratch -- lowering the bar for a durable resurgence.

insights.claim: The December 2023 hijacking of the Maltese-flagged MV Ruen -- the first successful Somali piracy hijacking in more than six years -- occurred just weeks after the Houthis began attacking Red Sea shipping and international naval assets were reallocated away from Somali waters to counter them.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: MV Ruen marks the specific inflection point where naval-attention diversion first re-enabled piracy, establishing the causal template (naval reallocation -> piracy reactivation) that repeated again in 2026 with the Iran war.

insights.claim: The March 2024 hijacking of the Bangladesh-flagged MV Abdullah, which pirates said yielded a $5 million ransom after 32 days of negotiation, was the first successful Somali piracy ransom collection in over a decade (since the 2012 MV Smyrna case) and proved the old hijack-anchor-negotiate-collect business model was still viable, effectively signaling to would-be pirates that piracy was profitable again ahead of the larger 2026 wave.
insights.speaker: narrator
insights.so_what: A single proven successful ransom collection functioned as a real-world proof-of-concept that reactivated investor and recruit interest in piracy, which is the direct precursor logic to the four hijackings that followed in 2026.
insights.quote: Reuters interviewed the pirates afterward who claimed that they had received a $5 million ransom payment from the ship owner following 32 days of negotiations.
